output.name: Hasket
output.myth: When Aun cut the string, Mother Hesk was spinning the thread that would have held the sky close. Her drop spindle slipped from her fingers in the wind and went up after the cut end, still turning. Tulma, the whorl, spun thread as it climbed. Kesin, the hook, caught on nothing. A gull was working the north ledges with a cod in its beak, and it watched the spindle go past. Sokul, the Stooping Gull, still watches that ledge from the south-west. Hesk did not stop her hands. She keeps count of the yarn it spun on the way up, in Tesuk, the Counting Hands, a fist and a half north of the spindle. Ennu says the thread is nearly long enough to reach the islands. Tavo says it is not, and laughs. Aun says nothing. He mends a net. When the thread is long enough, the old woman says, the spindle drops down the string and the sky comes home. Until then we spin our wool short and tie the ends. Mind your hands on the spindle when the wind is up.
output.finding: Find Tesuk, the Counting Hands, high in the north, and Hasket lies a fist and a half straight south of it.
